Looking for a babysitter
Valletta, April. Giulia and Matei work all day on the scaffolding. In the afternoons, after nursery, they need someone for Viola. Marija, Camilleri's wife, helps Giulia write an advert.
So, what shall we write? "Babysitter wanted…"
"…who speaks Italian." Viola only understands Maltese when biscuits are involved.
All right. "Who speaks Italian and is patient." Anything else?
Who knows a Romanian lullaby. The little one only falls asleep with that.
Giulia dear, there's nobody in Malta who knows a Romanian lullaby. Maybe not in the whole Mediterranean.
Then I'll sing it in the evenings. But at least someone who tells her stories.
Wait… I know a girl who studies at the university and tells wonderful stories. My niece Lina.
Does she speak Italian?
Better than me. She's the only one in the family who has studied in Florence. One year, on Erasmus.
In Florence? That's the nicest thing anyone has said to me since I've been here.
Then no advert. I'll bring her tomorrow. But I warn you: she's the chattiest person I know.
Perfect. With Viola you need someone who talks more than she does.

1. Relative clause with the indicative or the congiuntivo?
Indicative (real, known)
Congiuntivo (sought, hypothetical)
Conosco una ragazza che parla italiano.
Cerco una ragazza che parli italiano.
Ho un amico che sa cucinare.
Vorrei un amico che sappia cucinare.
C’è un ristorante che apre la domenica.
C’è un ristorante che apra la domenica?
The key question: do I know the person / thing exists? If yes, indicative. If I'm looking for it, wishing for it or unsure, congiuntivo. In English the difference is often invisible: "who speaks".
2. After negatives
Non c’è nessuno che sappia una ninna nanna rumena.
There's nobody who knows…
Non conosco niente che sia più bello.
I don't know anything more beautiful.
Non ho trovato un posto che mi piaccia.
I haven't found a place I like.
What is denied doesn't exist, so it's "unreal": hence the congiuntivo.
3. After superlatives
È il quadro più bello che io abbia mai visto.
È la persona più chiacchierona che io conosca.
She's the chattiest person I know.
Era il viaggio più lungo che avessimo mai fatto.
It was the longest journey we had ever made.
Note the sequence of tenses: main verb in the present → congiuntivo presente / passato (abbia visto); in the past → imperfetto / trapassato (avessimo fatto).
4. After l'unico, il solo, il primo, l'ultimo
È l’unica che abbia studiato a Firenze.
She's the only one who has studied in Florence.
Sei il solo che possa aiutarmi.
You're the only one who can help me.
È il primo che sia arrivato.
He's the first to have arrived.
È l’ultima cosa che mi aspettassi.
It's the last thing I expected.

In everyday speech you'll also hear the indicative after superlatives and after "l'unico" ("È il più bello che ho visto"). It's accepted in informal speech, but at B2 level and in writing use the congiuntivo.

Pietro sull’impalcatura

Lina arrived the next day, as promised, and she was exactly as Marija had described her: the chattiest person Giulia had ever met. She was twenty-two, with curly hair, a rucksack full of books and Italian with a Florentine accent, learned during her Erasmus year. After ten minutes she had already told Giulia her whole life story, and after twenty Viola had put her cloth bunny in her hands, something she had never done with anyone outside the family. "Hired," said Matei that evening. "She's the first person Viola has accepted so quickly."

There was another thing that made Lina special. On the first evening, putting Viola to bed, Giulia started singing Viorica's lullaby, as she did every evening. Lina, who was tidying the toys, stopped to listen. Then, at the second verse, she started humming along. Giulia looked at her in amazement. "You know it?" "No," answered Lina. "But my grandmother used to sing one with the same tune. In Maltese. She said she'd learned it from an old Romanian woman who worked at the port in the fifties." Giulia was speechless. Marija had been wrong: there was someone in Malta who knew that lullaby.

Work on the painting went on one millimetre at a time, as Bellini had taught. The first weeks were spent just looking: photographs with ultraviolet light, with infrared, with X-rays, hours and hours at the microscope. The chemist from Palermo analysed the pigments, the Japanese photographer took ten thousand shots, and Karl, the apprentice, learned to prepare the glues with a patience Giulia had never seen in any other boy his age, except one. "You remind me of a friend of mine in Florence," she told him one day. "His name is Davide. He never talks while he works either." Karl blushed. It was the nicest compliment he had ever received.

In Florence, meanwhile, the workshop carried on without them, and it was going well. Every Sunday at seven, punctual as Ion's watch, the video call came. Chiara reported on the work, Davide showed his drawings, Bellini commented from his corner, and at the end Graziella took the phone and sang Viorica's lullaby to Viola, with a Romanian-Florentine accent that made everyone laugh. One Sunday in May Chiara announced some news. She needed help with an embroidered silk altar cloth, and she was looking for someone who knew how to work with antique textiles. "There's nobody in the whole of Florence who has time," she sighed. "They're all in Rome for the Jubilee."

It was Doina, connected from Sibiu on the same video call, who solved the problem. "Me," she said in hesitant Italian. "I can work silk. I embroidered the costumes of the Sibiu theatre for forty years." There was a surprised silence. Nobody, not even Matei, knew his mother had worked for the theatre. "You never said," he said. Doina shrugged. "Nobody ever asked me." Two weeks later she was in Florence, with Ion, in a little flat Valeria had found in Via dei Serragli. Chiara said she was the best assistant she had ever had. Davide said she was the only person who could make him be quiet with a single look.

In mid-June, once school had finished, Pietro arrived. He was travelling alone for the first time in his life, with a tag round his neck saying "Unaccompanied minor" and a ticket given by Bellini. Graziella had gone with him as far as security at Pisa, with a flask labelled "herbal tea" which, this time, had been stopped. "Signora, this is ribollita," the officer had said. "I know," Graziella had replied. "But however good it is, the law is the law." The officer had confiscated the flask with the air of a man who had already planned his dinner.

At Malta airport Viola recognised Pietro from a distance and ran towards him shouting his name, which for her was still "Piè". Pietro picked her up and spun her round until they were both dizzy. Then he looked at Giulia and Matei, tanned, smiling, a little different from how he remembered them. "You've changed," he said. "You look Maltese." Matei laughed. "And you've grown taller than me," he replied. It was almost true. At nearly thirteen, Pietro had passed Marco's notch at thirteen, and now looked Giulia in the eye without raising his head.

The next day Giulia took him to the Co-Cathedral. Before going into the oratory, she gave him the same speech Camilleri had given them in February: "Don't look at the painting straight away. Look first at the floor, then at the walls, then raise your eyes slowly." Pietro obeyed. Giulia, beside him, saw him raise his eyes and saw his face change, as hers had changed four months earlier. For five minutes Pietro said nothing. Then he whispered, without turning round: "It's the most beautiful painting I have ever seen." And Giulia noticed, with a touch of pride, that he had used the subjunctive without thinking.

Camilleri, who had come in behind them, heard the sentence and smiled. Then he did something that wasn't allowed by the Co-Cathedral's rules. "Would you like to go up?" he asked Pietro, pointing at the scaffolding. Pietro looked at Giulia, who hesitated for a moment, then nodded. With a helmet on his head and Matei following him rung by rung, Pietro climbed to the top, five metres above the floor, level with the signature. From there the painting no longer looked like a painting. It looked like a room, dark and real, in which someone was about to die and nobody could do anything.

Giulia showed him the signature under the microscope. The cracks she had seen in February, thin as hairs, were now closed, consolidated one by one with Ernesto's brush. "It took me two months," she said. "For a piece the size of a postcard." Pietro looked into the microscope for a long time. Then he raised his head with a strange expression. "Giulia," he said softly, "there's something under the 'f'. A sort of dot. Like a smaller letter." Giulia laughed. "I know. Lots of people have noticed it. It's a drop of paint. Nobody has managed to work out what it is."

Pietro didn't answer. He looked again, adjusted the focus, then took from his pocket the notebook he always made notes in and copied, very carefully, the shape he could see: a small curve, a line, a dot. Then he stared at the page. "It looks like a 'T'," he said. "A tiny T, with a dot next to it." Matei and Giulia looked at each other. Camilleri, from below, asked what was going on. "Nothing," Giulia answered, too quickly. "The boy has a lot of imagination." But that evening, at dinner, none of the three could think of anything else.

"A T," Pietro kept saying, turning his fork among the pastizzi. "Like Totò." "Pietro," said Giulia patiently, "Caravaggio painted this picture in Malta in 1608. He painted Totò in Sicily, afterwards. There's no proof that…" She stopped. Matei had put down his glass. "Unless," he said slowly, "Totò had come with him. Rosalia Lo Bianco wrote that Agata, the washerwoman, was paid three tarì for her son. But she never found out where she and the boy came from. Nobody knows where they were before Syracuse."

Giulia was silent. Then she picked up her phone and wrote a message to Rosalia Lo Bianco, in Catania, whom she hadn't heard from for months: "Dear Rosalia, is there anyone in your archive who could look for a washerwoman called Agata in Malta in 1607 or 1608? It's the strangest hypothesis I've ever made, but a twelve-year-old boy has seen a T under Caravaggio's signature." The answer came ten minutes later, at eleven at night: "Dear Giulia, it's the craziest thing anyone has ever written to me. I'm taking the ferry tomorrow."

Rosalia arrived the next day with a suitcase full of photocopies and the same energy she'd had in Syracuse. She spent three days shut in the archives of the Order of Malta, with Pietro as her assistant, because he was the only one who never got tired of reading old handwriting. On the fourth day she came out of the archive with a sheet of paper in her hand and the face of someone who has seen a ghost. It was a copy of a register from the knights' hospital, from September 1608. Among the names of the poor treated that month was one line: "Agatha, lavandaria siciliana, cum filio Salvatore, annorum septem".

"Agata, Sicilian washerwoman, with her son Salvatore, aged seven," translated Rosalia, her voice trembling. "They were here. In Malta. In the same month Caravaggio was painting this picture." Pietro went red to the tips of his ears. Matei put a hand on his shoulder. Giulia looked at the painting, at the little T under the signature, and felt the same thing she had felt in Syracuse in front of the X-ray. "So it's not a coincidence," she said softly. "Totò was here. And Caravaggio, before fleeing, left his name in the saint's blood. And next to it, tiny, a child's initial."

"A hypothesis," said Camilleri, who had come running as soon as he heard the news. "A beautiful one, but a hypothesis. It will have to be studied for years." Then he looked at Pietro and smiled. "But it's the most beautiful hypothesis ever born in this oratory. And it was made by a twelve-year-old who climbed the scaffolding without permission." "With your permission," Pietro pointed out. "Exactly," replied Camilleri. "We'll put this in the record as my fault. That way, if one day it becomes famous, the glory is yours and the blame is mine."

That Sunday, at seven, the video call with Florence lasted two hours. Pietro told the whole story from the beginning, in order, with the right connectors, as he had learned at the meeting: first of all the T, then Rosalia, then the archive, finally the hospital register. When he had finished, there was a long silence on the other side of the screen. Then Bellini, in his corner of the workshop, took off his glasses. "My boy," he said, "you're the most stubborn person I have ever known. After your grandfather. He looked at paintings for hours without saying anything. You look at them for hours and then say the right thing."

Graziella, on the other hand, had only one question. She leaned towards the phone until all you could see on the screen was her nose and her glasses. "And the boy?" she asked. "Totò. In the hospital. Was he ill?" Rosalia, who was sitting next to Giulia, answered gently. "The register only says they were treated. And that three weeks later they left, both of them healed." Graziella nodded slowly, satisfied. "Good," she said. "Then someone fed him. Hot soup, I hope. It's the only thing that really matters when you're seven and far from home."

The next day Rosalia phoned Syracuse, to Turi, the old sacristan of Santa Lucia, who was nearly eighty and didn't use a computer. She told him everything: the T, the hospital, Agata and Salvatore in Malta. Turi listened without interrupting. Then he asked just one thing: whether the boy had recovered. Rosalia said yes. Then Turi was silent for a long moment, and in the end he said that that very evening he would light a candle in front of the painting, "for the Totò of Santa Lucia, who is now also the Totò of San Giovanni". Then he added that if anyone wanted to bring the Malta painting to Syracuse, he would have no objection. Rosalia laughed and explained that it wasn't possible. "Pity," said Turi. "Two Totòs under the same roof would have been the most beautiful thing I've ever seen."

On the last evening of his holiday, Pietro sat on the apartment terrace with Giulia and Matei, while Viola slept and Lina sang her the lullaby in Maltese. Below them the harbour glittered with lights. "You know," said Pietro, "in January, when you couldn't decide, I wrote seven arguments to convince you to go. But I was missing the eighth." "Which one?" asked Matei. Pietro smiled. "That if you hadn't come, nobody would ever have found the T. Consequently, I was right." Giulia laughed and ruffled his hair. "That," she said, "is the best argument I have ever heard."
